analysis.one_liner: Expires federal regulations after 10 years unless agencies formally re-issue them.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have put a 10-year expiration clock on all federal regulations, never got a committee hearing or a vote and died at the end of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal administrative law so that every regulation an agency issues expires 10 years later. To keep a rule in force, the agency would have to run the full notice-and-comment rulemaking process again, as if it were brand new. It would also make non-binding agency guidance subject to court review and route those cases to the federal appeals courts. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated businesses — banks, manufacturers, chemical and energy companies, and other firms subject to federal rules — would gain, because any rule an agency fails to re-issue on time simply expires, and the prospect of expiration gives companies leverage to oppose rules they dislike. Companies could also sue over agency guidance documents, which today cannot be challenged directly in court, adding another tool for delaying enforcement.

how_it_helps.text: Any rule an agency does not re-promulgate through full notice-and-comment procedures within 10 years automatically ceases to be effective, so industry opponents only need to run out the clock on an agency's bandwidth to make a rule disappear.
The bill expands 'final agency action' to include interpretive rules, general statements of policy, and procedural rules, making this guidance directly challengeable in court for the first time.
It gives federal courts of appeals exclusive jurisdiction to review rules that have expired but are still being enforced, concentrating challenges in a venue favorable to well-resourced litigants.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal protections — from workplace safety and clean air to financial consumer rules — bear the risk that a rule lapses because an agency missed the 10-year deadline or was forced to divert staff to re-issuing old rules instead of enforcing them. Agencies also pay, in the form of a massive ongoing workload of re-doing old rulemakings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Agencies and people relying on federal rules

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to every rule promulgated after enactment, so agencies would face a rolling wave of expiring rules and would have to spend resources re-issuing longstanding, uncontroversial rules rather than writing new ones or enforcing existing ones.

A rule that an agency fails to re-issue before its expiration date simply stops being effective, creating gaps in enforcement — for example, a pollution limit or safety standard could lapse and leave the public unprotected until re-issued.

Making policy statements and interpretive rules subject to court review would expose agencies to more litigation over documents that are currently not binding, slowing down day-to-day government guidance.

Supporters would argue the sunset forces agencies to periodically justify old rules with fresh evidence and public input, retiring outdated or burdensome regulations that otherwise linger indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea of periodically re-examining old rules has some appeal, but the design is lopsided: it applies a hard expiration to all rules regardless of whether they are outdated, and the remedy for a missed deadline is that the rule vanishes rather than stays in place while the agency catches up. Combined with expanded litigation over agency guidance, the practical effect would be to shift agency time from protecting the public toward defending and re-issuing old rules — a benefit mainly to regulated firms that want rules off the books.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2015 and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it, so it died quietly when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Steve Daines introduced the REVIEWS Act on March 19, 2015, with no cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill mainly served regulated industries seeking to put expiration pressure on federal rules, its death means agencies kept their existing authority to maintain and enforce regulations without a 10-year re-approval treadmill — so the public that relies on those rules is no worse off, and regulated businesses gained nothing they could not get through ordinary lobbying against individual rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the public relying on their rules

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single sponsor with no cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (banks, manufacturers, energy and chemical companies, and other firms subject to federal rules)
industries.note: A 10-year expiration on every rule would let industry opponents outlast agencies: if an agency cannot complete a fresh rulemaking in time, the rule disappears. Expanded court review of agency guidance would add another venue to contest enforcement. The public benefit these rules deliver (clean air, workplace safety, consumer finance protection) would be put at risk to create this leverage.

Agencies would have to re-run notice-and-comment rulemaking for every existing rule every decade, diverting staff and budgets from enforcement and new protections. The bill's expanded judicial-review provisions would also increase litigation against them.
